items.stem: Which of these are health metrics a clinic might record at a checkup? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Health metrics are measurable facts about the body or habits, like blood pressure, heart rate, and height and weight.
options: Favorite music genre
Blood pressure
Resting heart rate
Number of social media followers
Height and weight

items.stem: Sort each fictional person's result as a positive health metric or one that needs attention.
items.rationale: Positive metrics fall in healthy ranges for a teen; repeated readings outside those ranges are a signal to follow up.
options: Positive metric
Needs attention
rows: Sleeps about 5 hours on school nights
Blood pressure far above the normal range at repeated visits
Resting heart rate of 68 beats per minute
Sleeps 9 hours on most school nights

items.stem: Jamal's blood pressure was a little high at one visit. Which statement about reading health metrics is most accurate?
items.rationale: Metrics are most useful when tracked over time and interpreted by a professional in context.
options: Every person has exactly the same healthy range, no matter their age.
A reading outside the range means the person is definitely sick.
One number always tells the whole story of a person's health.
One reading is one piece of information; trends over time and a health professional's interpretation matter.

items.stem: Sort each lifestyle factor by whether it generally supports health or diminishes it.
items.rationale: Activity and balanced eating support health metrics; inactivity and chronic sleep loss work against them.
options: Supports health
Diminishes health
rows: Long stretches of sitting with little movement
Regularly getting too little sleep
Regular physical activity
Eating a variety of fruits and vegetables

items.stem: Dana (fictional) sleeps 5 hours a night and sits most evenings. Which change would most likely improve her health metrics?
items.rationale: Regular movement and enough sleep are lifestyle changes that improve many health metrics at once.
options: Drink an energy drink every afternoon to stay alert.
Stop checking any health numbers.
Move more during the day and go to bed earlier.
Skip breakfast so she has more time to sleep.

items.stem: Which of these are physical health metrics? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Physical metrics measure the body and its habits, such as sleep, heart rate, and activity.
options: Hours of sleep per night
How well a person handles disappointment
Minutes of physical activity per day
Resting heart rate
How many people they feel close to

items.stem: Which is the best example of a mental health metric?
items.rationale: Mental health metrics describe thinking, focus, stress, and coping rather than the body or relationships.
options: How well a person can concentrate and cope with everyday stress
Number of steps taken per day
A blood pressure reading
Number of friends a person has

items.stem: A fictional student sleeps poorly and then has trouble focusing and feels irritable. What does this show about wellness?
items.rationale: Physical habits like sleep influence mental and emotional wellness, so the dimensions are linked.
options: The dimensions of wellness are connected and affect each other.
Each dimension of wellness works completely on its own.
Mood is only affected by what a person eats.
Only physical health matters for doing well in school.

items.stem: Priya (fictional) often feels left out and has no one to talk to when school is hard. Which dimension of wellness is mostly affected?
items.rationale: Having supportive relationships and someone to talk to are social wellness metrics.
options: Social wellness
Financial wellness
Environmental wellness
Physical wellness

items.stem: Sort each example by the dimension it best shows.
items.rationale: Social wellness is about relationships; emotional wellness is about understanding and managing feelings.
options: Social wellness
Emotional wellness
rows: Notices when feeling overwhelmed and uses a coping skill
Has at least one trusted person to talk with
Can name feelings and handle disappointment without lashing out
Treats others with respect and communicates clearly

items.stem: What is the main purpose of a personal wellness self-assessment?
items.rationale: A self-assessment is a reflection tool; it is not a test, a diagnosis, or a ranking.
options: To reflect honestly on current habits and find strengths and areas to improve
To prove that a person is already healthy
To diagnose a medical condition
To earn a grade that is compared with other students

items.stem: Maya's (fictional) self-assessment shows sleep 2 out of 5, physical activity 4 out of 5, and stress 3 out of 5. What are her strength and her area to improve?
items.rationale: Her highest score is a strength and her lowest score is the clearest area to work on.
options: Strength: physical activity. Area to improve: sleep.
She has no strengths because no score is 5.
Strength: stress. Area to improve: physical activity.
Strength: sleep. Area to improve: physical activity.

items.stem: Match each description to the SMART letter it shows.
items.rationale: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.
options: Specific
Measurable
Achievable
Relevant
Time-bound
rows: Has a deadline: by the end of May
Realistic for your schedule and resources
Names exactly what you will do: drink water with lunch
Includes a number you can track: 20 minutes
Matters for your own wellness needs

items.stem: A goal says, "Be healthier." Which revision fixes the missing SMART parts?
items.rationale: The revision names the action, a number, a realistic plan, and a time frame.
options: Exercise a lot more and eat better soon.
Run a marathon next week.
Walk 20 minutes after school on 4 days a week for the next 6 weeks.
Never eat sweets again starting tomorrow.

items.stem: Which of these goals include all five SMART parts? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: A SMART goal names a specific action, a measure, a realistic target, a reason, and a deadline.
options: Sleep 8 hours on school nights, Sunday to Thursday, for the next month to help focus in class.
Drink 6 cups of water a day for two weeks to reduce afternoon headaches.
Lose a lot of weight fast.
Be less stressed.

items.stem: Which are warning signs that a health claim may be misleading? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Quick-fix promises, testimonials instead of evidence, and a sales motive are common red flags.
options: Uses only before-and-after photos and personal testimonials as proof
Promises fast results with no effort, like "lose 15 pounds in 10 days"
Cites a named study and links to it
Sells a product while giving the advice
Is reviewed by a medical organization

items.stem: Sort each feature by whether it points to a credible source or a source to question.
items.rationale: Credible sources show expertise and evidence; popularity and a sales motive do not make a source credible.
options: Credible source
Question this source
rows: An influencer with many followers who sells supplements
Cites research and names its authors
Anonymous post with no sources
A government health agency or university medical center

items.stem: A fitness influencer with millions of followers says a tea "melts belly fat." What does their popularity show?
items.rationale: Follower counts and appearance are not evidence; credibility comes from expertise and reliable proof.
options: Nothing about whether the claim is true; credibility depends on evidence and expertise.
The claim must be true because so many people follow them.
The claim is true if many comments agree with it.
The claim is true if the influencer looks fit.

items.stem: Which is the best way to check a health claim you saw on social media?
items.rationale: Verifying means checking the claim against reliable, independent sources, not repeating it.
options: Share it and see whether friends believe it.
Compare it with credible sources such as the CDC, NIH, or a medical center.
Search for another post that says the same thing.
Trust it if the video looks professionally made.

items.stem: A fictional ad claims a supplement "burns fat while you sleep." Which decision and reason are best?
items.rationale: A good justification points to missing evidence and the seller's motive, not to reviews or blanket distrust.
options: Do not trust it yet: there is no evidence given, and the seller profits from the claim.
Do not trust it: ads are always lies.
Trust it: the ad has lots of five-star reviews.
Trust it: supplements are always tested for safety and results.

items.stem: Sam (fictional) has a big test tomorrow. It is 11:30 p.m. and friends invite him to play online. What decision must Sam make?
items.rationale: The decision is the choice Sam must make now, which affects his rest and his test.
options: Whether to take the test
Whether to stay up playing or go to sleep before the test
Whether his friends are good friends
Which game is the most fun

items.stem: Lena is exhausted, has homework left, and friends want to hang out online. Which are realistic choices she could make? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Good options are realistic and fit her responsibilities; ignoring the situation is not a choice that solves it.
options: Tell her friends she will connect tomorrow
Ignore everything and hope it works out
Stay up all night doing both
Play online for a short, set time, then stop and go to bed
Finish homework, then go to bed on time

items.stem: Sort each consequence of regularly staying up very late on school nights.
items.rationale: Choices often have short-term benefits and longer-term costs, and both belong in the decision.
options: Positive consequence
Negative consequence
rows: Finishing a game or show you enjoy
Feeling tired and irritable over time
More time to relax with friends tonight
Trouble focusing in class tomorrow

items.stem: Using the STOP steps, which choice is the most responsible for a tired student with a test tomorrow?
items.rationale: A responsible choice considers consequences for health and responsibilities.
options: Skip the test preparation altogether.
Stay up as late as friends are online.
Set a stopping time, finish what is necessary, and get enough sleep.
Do whatever an adult says without thinking.

items.stem: Which reasoning best explains why a choice is a responsible health decision?
items.rationale: Responsible decisions are based on consequences and ownership, not on pleasing others or perfection.
options: It is the choice that is perfect in every way.
It is what most of my friends are doing.
It weighs the likely short- and long-term consequences for my health and responsibilities.
It is what an adult told me to do.

items.stem: Which statement best defines mental health?
items.rationale: Everyone has mental health; it is part of overall wellness, not just the absence of illness.
options: Another term for mental illness
The absence of any mental illness
Feeling happy all of the time
A person's emotional, psychological, and social well-being: how they think, feel, and handle daily life

items.stem: Why is mental health better described as a continuum than as "healthy" or "mentally ill"?
items.rationale: A continuum shows that mental health shifts with experiences, support, and stress.
options: A person is either mentally healthy or mentally ill and stays that way.
Only people with a diagnosis fall anywhere on the range.
People move along a range from thriving to struggling, and where they are can change over time.
Mental health is set at birth and never changes.

items.stem: Which statements are true about what can influence teen mental health? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Family, peers, school, media, and life experiences all influence mental health; willpower alone is not the whole story.
options: Sleep and daily routines can affect it
Willpower is the only thing that matters; outside experiences have no effect
Supportive family and friends can protect it
It is fixed at birth and nothing can influence it
Social media experiences can influence it
Ongoing bullying or conflict can harm it

items.stem: Sort each factor for a fictional teen as a risk factor or a protective factor.
items.rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of struggling; protective factors, like connectedness, help buffer stress.
options: Risk factor
Protective factor
rows: Feeling close to family
Being bullied at school
Feeling connected to a school team or club
Ongoing lack of sleep

items.stem: Which of these statements are inaccurate? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: These myths add stigma; stress can be helpful in small amounts and counseling is a healthy step.
options: Stress is always harmful.
Seeking counseling means someone cannot handle their own problems.
Mental health can change throughout a person's life.
A person with a diagnosed mental illness can still function well.
People with mental illness are always visibly struggling.

items.stem: Which fictional student's situation most likely suggests a need for extra support?
items.rationale: Feelings that last for weeks and interfere with daily life go beyond an everyday challenge.
options: Feels sad for a day after a game loss
Feels tired after a very busy week
Feels nervous the night before a test
Has avoided friends and struggled to get out of bed for several weeks

items.stem: Which could be warning signs that a person needs help? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Lasting changes in behavior, mood, and daily functioning are warning signs; occasional nerves are normal.
options: Feeling nervous before a performance
A sudden drop in schoolwork
Talking about feeling hopeless
Wanting some quiet time after a long day
Pulling away from friends and activities
Big changes in sleep or appetite

items.stem: Which part of the Duration, Intensity, Interference check does each detail show?
items.rationale: How long, how strong, and how much it disrupts daily life all help decide the level of concern.
options: Duration
Intensity
Interference
rows: Worry is so strong it causes panic
Has not felt like himself for months
Has felt this way most days for six weeks
Can no longer focus on homework or go to practice

items.stem: A fictional student shows several warning signs. Which is the most appropriate source of support?
items.rationale: Counselors and trusted adults can assess the situation and connect the student to the right help.
options: An anonymous online forum
Waiting to see if it goes away on its own
A social media influencer's coping video
A school counselor or another trusted adult

items.stem: Why should a peer recognize and refer instead of trying to diagnose a friend?
items.rationale: Peers notice and refer; diagnosing is for professionals.
options: A friend can diagnose if they have read about it online.
Warning signs only matter after a diagnosis.
Only trained professionals can diagnose; a friend's job is to notice changes and connect the person to help.
Naming the disorder is the most helpful thing a friend can do.

items.stem: What happens in the body during the basic stress (fight-or-flight) response?
items.rationale: The stress response activates the body, and recovery afterward is important.
options: The body shuts down to rest until the stressor passes.
Heart rate and breathing speed up as the body prepares to react.
Heart rate and breathing slow down to save energy.
Only the mind is affected, not the body.

items.stem: Sort each coping behavior as generally helpful or potentially harmful.
items.rationale: Helpful coping addresses stress or helps the body recover; harmful coping avoids it or adds new risks.
options: Generally helpful
Potentially harmful
rows: Slow, controlled breathing
Talking with a trusted person
Avoiding responsibilities and doomscrolling
Using alcohol or drugs to escape

items.stem: Which are evidence-informed coping strategies? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Breathing, movement, relaxation, and realistic thinking help; avoidance and lost sleep make stress worse.
options: A short walk or other movement
Avoiding the problem completely
Progressive muscle relaxation
Staying up all night to make up for lost time
Replacing "I'm going to fail" with a more realistic thought
Slow, controlled breathing

items.stem: Alex (fictional) has a big game tomorrow and feels jittery. Which strategy fits best?
items.rationale: Calming the body fits a stressor that is about nerves; avoidance does not address it.
options: Controlled breathing and a short walk to calm the body
Staying up late rewatching old games
Skipping practice to avoid the pressure
Scrolling for hours to avoid thinking about it

items.stem: Which coping plan for a fictional student is the most realistic and complete?
items.rationale: A realistic plan matches strategies to stressors, includes support, and knows when to get more help.
options: Handles everything alone without telling anyone
Uses one strategy every time, no matter the stressor
Names warning signs, two or three strategies, a person to talk to, and when to ask an adult for more help
Plans to never feel stress again

items.stem: Which show active listening? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Active listening means attention, patience, and checking understanding before offering ideas.
options: Telling a story about your own bigger problem
Immediately giving advice
Giving full attention and putting your phone away
Letting the person finish without interrupting
Repeating back what you heard to check you understood

items.stem: Sort each response to a struggling friend as supportive or dismissive.
items.rationale: Supportive language validates feelings; dismissive language minimizes them.
options: Supportive
Dismissive
rows: That sounds really difficult.
Other people have it worse.
I'm glad you told me.
Just get over it.

items.stem: After listening to a friend who is struggling, which response best connects them to support?
items.rationale: Offering to connect and accompany a friend to a trusted adult is a safe, supportive step.
options: "Post about it online to get advice."
"You should just handle it yourself."
"I'll fix this for you."
"Would you be willing to talk to the school counselor? I can go with you."

items.stem: A friend asks you to keep a secret. In which situations must you involve a trusted adult? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Safety comes before secrecy when someone may be hurt.
options: A friend talks about hurting themselves
A friend says they plan to hurt someone
A friend is stressed about an upcoming test
A friend is being hurt or abused
A friend had an argument with a sibling

items.stem: A friend keeps coming to you with serious struggles. Which statement is accurate?
items.rationale: Friends are support, not treatment; professionals and trusted adults provide the help.
options: You should promise to keep everything secret no matter what.
If they do not improve, it is your fault.
Supporting someone means listening and connecting them to help, not treating or fixing the problem yourself.
A good friend becomes their therapist.

items.stem: Which are sources of mental-health support for teens? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Counselors, health providers, trusted adults, and crisis lines are reliable supports.
options: An anonymous comment section
An advertisement promising a quick cure
A school counselor
The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
A primary-care provider
A trusted parent, coach, or teacher

items.stem: Sort each resource as crisis support or non-crisis support.
items.rationale: Crisis resources are for immediate danger; non-crisis resources support ongoing needs.
options: Crisis support
Non-crisis support
rows: Calling 911 in an immediate emergency
Talking with the school counselor about ongoing stress
Scheduling regular visits with a therapist
988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

items.stem: Which source is most likely to give credible mental-health information?
items.rationale: Credible information comes from experts and evidence-based organizations.
options: An influencer selling a supplement
A government health agency or major medical organization, like the CDC or NIH
An anonymous forum post
An ad promising a quick cure

items.stem: Noah (fictional) has felt down for weeks but is not in danger. Which resource fits best?
items.rationale: Ongoing, non-emergency concerns match counselors and health providers.
options: Calling 911
Wait until it becomes an emergency
Strangers' advice in an online post
A school counselor or primary-care provider to talk and plan next steps

items.stem: Sort each strategy by the barrier to getting help it helps overcome.
items.rationale: Naming the barrier makes it easier to choose a strategy that works.
options: Stigma or embarrassment
Cost or transportation
Not knowing where to go
rows: Ask a trusted adult to help arrange rides or appointments
Ask the school counselor about free or low-cost options
Remember that asking for help is common and a sign of strength
Check the school's resource list to see who to contact

items.stem: Which of these can influence the health of a community? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Community conditions like air, water, care, food, and safe spaces all shape health alongside personal choices.
options: Access to healthcare
Nothing, because health is decided only by genes
Access to affordable healthy food
Nothing, because health is decided only by each person's choices
Air and water quality
Safe places to be physically active

items.stem: Sort each example as an individual health behavior or an environmental influence.
items.rationale: Behaviors are personal choices; environmental influences are conditions around a person that make choices easier or harder.
options: Individual behavior
Environmental influence
rows: Deciding what to eat for lunch
Whether a grocery store with fresh food is nearby
Whether safe sidewalks exist on the route to school
Choosing to walk to school

items.stem: Sort each feature of a fictional neighborhood as a risk factor or a protective factor.
items.rationale: Risk factors raise the chance of poor health outcomes; protective factors support health.
options: Risk factor
Protective factor
rows: A free community health clinic
No bus service to the clinic
A park with walking paths
A busy highway next to the homes

items.stem: A fictional neighborhood has no grocery store within five miles. How could this condition influence health?
items.rationale: Conditions can make healthy choices easier or harder without determining one person's outcome.
options: Residents may find it harder to get fresh, affordable food, which can affect nutrition over time.
It only affects adults.
It has no effect because food choices are entirely personal.
It guarantees that everyone there will become ill.

items.stem: Clinics and grocery stores are nearby, but residents lack reliable transportation. Which intervention is the most realistic and best justified?
items.rationale: A good intervention targets the actual barrier identified in the scenario.
options: Expand a bus route that connects the neighborhood to the clinic and grocery store, because transportation is the barrier.
Build another hospital, even though one is nearby.
Open a luxury gym.
Tell residents to walk farther.

items.stem: Which best describes the difference between healthcare and public health?
items.rationale: Healthcare focuses on individual patients, while public health works at the population level.
options: Public health only handles emergencies.
They are the same thing.
Healthcare mainly treats individuals; public health protects and improves the health of whole populations.
Public health treats individual patients in hospitals; healthcare protects populations.

items.stem: Which are functions of public-health agencies? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Surveillance, prevention, outbreak response, and preparedness protect whole communities.
options: Performing surgery on individual patients
Writing prescriptions for each patient
Promoting vaccination and prevention programs
Responding to outbreaks
Preparing for emergencies
Tracking disease patterns (surveillance)

items.stem: Match each problem to the group most likely to respond.
items.rationale: Individual care goes to providers; local problems go to local departments; multi-state problems involve the CDC.
options: Doctor or hospital
Local health department
CDC (federal)
rows: A student needs treatment for an ear infection
Running vaccination clinics for a county
Inspecting restaurants after several people in one town get sick
Tracking a measles outbreak spreading across many states

items.stem: Match each question to the part of STOP (Source, Timeliness, Objective, Proof) it checks.
items.rationale: STOP helps judge a source's authority, timing, purpose, and evidence.
options: Source
Timeliness
Objective
Proof
rows: Is the information from a health agency or expert?
Does it cite data or research?
Is the creator trying to sell or persuade?
Is the information current?

items.stem: Data show a higher asthma rate in Neighborhood A than in Neighborhood B. What does the data alone show?
items.rationale: A disparity shows a difference exists; it does not prove why.
options: That the data must be wrong
That pollution is the cause
That people in A make worse choices
A difference in outcomes; more information is needed before explaining the cause.

items.stem: Which are common environmental health hazards? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Air pollution, UV, loud noise, and heat can all harm health.
options: UV radiation from the sun
Drinking water from a tested, safe supply
Excessive noise
Extreme heat
Walking outdoors when air quality is good
Air pollution

items.stem: Match each example to hazard, exposure, or risk.
items.rationale: A hazard can cause harm, exposure is contact with it, and risk is the likelihood and severity of harm.
options: Hazard
Exposure
Risk
rows: The chance of sunburn or skin damage
Strong UV radiation from the midday sun
Water contaminated with lead
Working outside at noon without sunscreen

items.stem: One student uses earbuds at low volume for 30 minutes. Another uses them at very high volume for hours every day. Whose hearing risk is higher?
items.rationale: Risk depends on intensity, duration, and frequency, not just the presence of a hazard.
options: The same, because both use earbuds.
The second student: higher intensity, longer duration, and more frequent exposure raise risk.
Neither, because music cannot harm hearing.
The first student, because lower volume is more damaging.

items.stem: Today's Air Quality Index (AQI) is 160, which credible guidance labels "Unhealthy." What is the best interpretation?
items.rationale: At an AQI in the Unhealthy range, everyone may feel effects and sensitive groups are at greater risk.
options: Everyone should reduce long or heavy outdoor exertion, and people with asthma should take extra care.
AQI only matters for machines.
Only people who smoke are affected.
The air is safe for all activity.

items.stem: A soccer tournament is scheduled on a day with poor air quality. Which protective behaviors are realistic? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Risk can be reduced with practical steps even when the hazard cannot be removed.
options: Check the AQI before and during the event
Take more breaks and watch for symptoms
Play harder to finish faster
Ignore the air quality because nothing can be done
Shorten games or lower the intensity

items.stem: A fictional sports drink ad uses upbeat pop music, teen athletes, and social media influencers. Who is the intended audience?
items.rationale: Music, models, and platforms show who the advertiser wants to reach.
options: Teenagers and young adults
Doctors
Older adults
Young children

items.stem: Match each ad line to the persuasive technique it uses.
items.rationale: Advertisers use proof from the crowd, famous faces, urgency, and fear to persuade.
options: Social proof
Celebrity or influencer endorsement
Scarcity
Fear
rows: "Join the 2 million teens who already switched!"
A famous athlete holds the product
"Without this, you're falling behind your teammates."
"Only 50 left. Limited edition!"

items.stem: An ad shows a smiling athlete holding a sugary drink but never states that it improves performance. What is the implied message?
items.rationale: Ads can communicate implied messages without making an explicit claim.
options: That it is the cheapest drink
There is no message because no claim is stated
That drinking it will help you become athletic and successful
That it is made with only water

items.stem: Many students believe "everyone stays up past midnight on school nights," but a survey shows most do not. How can this belief affect behavior?
items.rationale: People often follow what they think is normal, even when they are wrong about it.
options: It only affects people who disagree.
It cannot, because only facts influence behavior.
Perceived norms can push people to act like others, even when the perception is inaccurate.
It only matters if the belief is true.

items.stem: A fast-food chain advertises discount meals to teens on many platforms every day. How could the repeated messages affect community health behaviors?
items.rationale: Repeated exposure can shape norms and choices across a community without determining any one person's decision.
options: It only affects people who already like the product.
It guarantees every teen will buy it.
Repetition has no effect; people only decide based on facts.
They can make the product seem normal, familiar, and appealing, influencing what many people choose.

items.stem: Which is the clearest, most specific community-health problem statement?
items.rationale: A clear problem names who is affected and what the harm is.
options: Health is bad.
People should be healthier.
Many students at our school listen to music at unsafe volumes, risking hearing damage.
Noise exists.

items.stem: For the problem of unsafe listening volume at school, which intervention is the most specific and realistic?
items.rationale: A good intervention is specific, feasible, and linked to the problem.
options: A volume-awareness campaign with posters and a free hearing-screening day at school
Make everyone healthier
Tell students to care more
Ban all music

items.stem: To get crosswalk lights installed near a school, which is the best audience for an advocacy message?
items.rationale: Advocacy targets people with the power to act.
options: The city council or transportation department, who can decide and fund it
Students who already agree
A celebrity with no connection to the town
Anyone who happens to see a social media post

items.stem: Which is a clear call to action?
items.rationale: A call to action names who should do what and by when.
options: We ask the school board to approve water bottle filling stations by next semester.
We hope people think about hydration.
Someone should do something about water.
Water is important for everyone.

items.stem: Which could show that a hearing-safety campaign worked? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Success is measured by changes in behavior or outcomes, not by effort or appearance.
options: The share of students using volume limits at a follow-up check
The number of posters printed
A student survey on listening volume before and after
How colorful the posters look

items.stem: Match each fictional example to tolerance, physical dependence, or addiction.
items.rationale: Tolerance and physical dependence are body adaptations; addiction involves compulsive use despite harm, so they are not the same.
options: Tolerance
Physical dependence
Addiction (substance use disorder)
rows: The body adjusts so the same dose no longer works as well
Needing larger amounts to get the same effect
Continuing to use despite repeated harm and loss of control
A patient takes prescribed pain medicine as directed and has withdrawal symptoms when it stops, with no compulsive use

items.stem: How can psychoactive substances affect brain function or behavior? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Substances alter brain signaling and can change judgment, coordination, mood, and memory.
options: They can change how brain cells communicate
They can affect mood and memory
They always cause permanent damage after one use
They can impair judgment and coordination
They affect behavior only when a large amount is used

items.stem: Which statements about substance-use risk are accurate? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Risk comes from many interacting factors; no single factor decides the outcome.
options: Many factors together influence risk, such as stress, genetics, and availability
Supportive family and friends can reduce risk
Addiction is just a lack of willpower
Any single risk factor guarantees addiction
Starting at a younger age raises the risk of problems

items.stem: Why can adolescents be more vulnerable to risk-taking?
items.rationale: Adolescent brain development makes reward-seeking strong while self-control is still maturing.
options: Teens cannot learn from consequences.
Teen brains are fully developed, so risk comes only from choices.
The brain systems for planning and impulse control are still developing while reward systems are highly active.
Impulse control develops before the reward system.

items.stem: Which source is best for supporting a claim about how addiction affects the brain?
items.rationale: Credible claims are backed by expert, evidence-based organizations.
options: NIDA (National Institute on Drug Abuse) or another NIH or CDC page
A website selling a detox product
A friend's opinion
A viral video from an anonymous account

items.stem: Why is nicotine especially concerning for teens?
items.rationale: The developing brain is more vulnerable to nicotine's effects and to dependence.
options: Teen brains are not affected by nicotine.
It is highly addictive and can affect attention, learning, and impulse control while the brain is still developing.
Nicotine is only harmful in cigarettes.
Nicotine only matters after many years of use.

items.stem: Which are health risks linked to tobacco or vaping? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Nicotine, aerosol chemicals, and smoke are linked to addiction, lung harm, brain effects, and cancer.
options: Better focus in the long run
Effects on attention and learning
Improved lung capacity
Nicotine addiction
Irritation and harm to the lungs
Cancer risk from toxic chemicals in burned tobacco

The brain stops developing
Changes in social interests
Hormonal changes
Mood and emotional changes

Controlling who the other person can talk to

Asking repeatedly until someone agrees is fine.
